claims.text: The new approach explicitly models atomic-scale disorder and defect effects in HfNbTaTiZr.
The new approach decouples lattice and electronic heat transport.
The approach will predict lattice thermal conductivity about 20–30% closer to experiment than previous DFT-based perfect-crystal estimates.
From 300 to 1200 K, the lattice contribution is significantly lower than earlier conflated estimates.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions are comparable.
HfNbTaTiZr is assumed to be in a single-phase, well-controlled state with oxygen contamination no greater than 1 wt.%.
The framework incorporates temperature-dependent phonon scattering, oxygen-defect effects, and machine-learning-corrected force constants.
The experimentally measured total thermal conductivity from 300 to 1200 K is 10–17 W/(K·m).
Atomic-scale disorder and oxygen-related defect interactions modify phonon-scattering rates and force constants.
Separately accounting for temperature-dependent defect and disorder effects on phonon scattering refines lattice thermal-conductivity predictions.
Earlier methods assume a perfect crystal and conflate lattice and electronic transport channels.
Decoupling lattice vibrations from electronic effects leads to more accurate predictions.
At high temperature, the predicted lattice thermal conductivity will be lower than prior estimates by roughly 20–30%.
Combining the predicted lattice and electronic contributions will yield total conductivity within 10–17 W/(K·m).
Below 200 K, the model will reproduce experimentally observed divergent trends in lattice and electronic contributions.
Earlier DFT, Debye, and perfect-crystal approximations have larger deviations from experiment.
The model is applicable to bulk, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen at or below 1 wt.% in the ranges below 200 K and 300–1200 K.
Model accuracy may diminish at higher oxygen contents or in multiphase material.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis defines 20–30% as an improvement in closeness to experiment, whereas the predicted outcome also treats 20–30% as the amount by which lattice conductivity is lower than prior estimates. Relative error reduction and conductivity reduction are different quantities and need not coincide.

The model is claimed to improve on prior approaches by 20–30%, but the falsification rule only tests whether experiment lies within ±20–30% of the new prediction. It does not compare prediction errors from the new and prior approaches, so it cannot decisively test the stated relative improvement.
